enrichment.short_title: Auctioneer liability for returning unsold stolen painting
key_facts: A Jan Steen painting stolen from the claimant in 1979 was consigned to Christie's by a third party and offered at auction in 1997.
The painting was unsold and Christie's returned it to the consignor, acting in good faith and without notice of the theft.
The claimant's conversion and bailment claim was struck out for disclosing no reasonable cause of action.
On appeal the court proceeded on the basis that Christie's had acted in good faith and without notice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the High Court upholding a strike-out of the claimant's conversion and bailment claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Christie's was not liable in conversion or bailment for returning unsold goods to the apparent owner.
enrichment.ratio: An auctioneer who receives goods in good faith and without notice, offers them for sale but returns them unsold to the consignor does not commit conversion because liability generally requires a sale followed by delivery; contractual rights such as liens or powers of sale do not amount to conversion unless exercised, and no bailment duty is owed to an unknown true owner.
legal_issues: Whether cataloguing, marketing and returning an unsold painting amounts to conversion
Whether Christie's contractual lien and power of sale made receipt of the painting a pledge under section 11(2) of the 1977 Act
Whether Christie's owed bailment or equivalent duties to the true owner of whom it had no knowledge
Whether contractual terms with the consignor can themselves amount to conversion against the true owner

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review to quash police caution
key_facts: Mr Aru received a formal police caution for section 5 Public Order Act 1986 offences after arrest in Liverpool.
He alleged officers strip-searched him and pressured him in his cell to accept a caution rather than face court.
The custody sergeant properly administered the caution and the claimant signed forms admitting the offence.
Cross-examination of police witnesses was permitted because the outcome turned on disputed facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review to quash a police caution, with permission for witness cross-examination.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the claimant failed to prove improper conduct by the arresting officers.
enrichment.ratio: A caution may be quashed if Home Office cautioning rules are breached, but where the custody sergeant properly obtained admission and explained consequences, alleged prior improper pressure must be proved to the civil standard and serious allegations against officers require cogent evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Home Office cautioning conditions on admission and informed consent were satisfied
Whether alleged strip search and cell pressure invalidated the caution
Standard of proof for disputed factual allegations in judicial review
Whether the court could order recovery of costs from damages in a separate civil claim

enrichment.short_title: Statutory nuisance abatement notice at sewage works
key_facts: Hounslow served an abatement notice on Thames Water for odour nuisance from Mogden Sewage Treatment Works.
A magistrates' court quashed the notice, holding sewage works were excluded from section 79(1)(d) following R v Parlby.
Thames Water appealed by way of case stated, arguing the 1990 Act restatement brought sewage works within subsection (1)(d).
The works treated about 500 million litres of wastewater daily as an industrial treatment process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from a magistrates' court decision quashing a statutory nuisance abatement notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sewage treatment works can fall within section 79(1)(d) and the matter was remitted to the magistrates' court.
enrichment.ratio: The Parlby construction of 'premises in such a state' under predecessor provisions applies only to section 79(1)(a) and should not be extended to section 79(1)(d), whose separate legislative history and plain words cover smell arising on industrial premises used for treatment or process, subject to the best practicable means defence.
legal_issues: Whether Mogden Sewage Treatment Works are 'premises' for section 79(1)(d)
Whether R v Parlby excludes sewage works from the Environmental Protection Act 1990
Whether 'premises' must bear the same meaning throughout section 79
Whether policy considerations from the 1875 public health legislation still apply

key_facts: The claimant suffered a serious groin injury falling from a site storage platform on 1 July 1994.
Proceedings were issued on 19 June 2001, nearly four years after the three-year limitation period expired.
Delay was caused by successive solicitors and counsel failing to issue in time, not by the illiterate claimant.
The judge disapplied limitation under section 33, finding actual prejudice to the defendant slight and a fair trial still possible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a first-instance order under section 33 of the Limitation Act 1980 disapplying the limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's exercise of discretion under section 33 was not plainly wrong.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 33 the court asks whether it is equitable to allow a stale claim having regard to all circumstances in section 33(3); an appellate court should not interfere unless the decision exceeds reasonable disagreement, and a blameless claimant's advisers' delay does not automatically displace a defendant's prejudice where a fair trial remains possible.
legal_issues: Whether seven years' delay in a personal injury claim justified refusing section 33 relief
Extent of prejudice from lost insurer files and faded witness memories
Whether claimant conduct includes solicitors' incompetence after instructions were given
Appropriate appellate standard for reviewing section 33 discretion

enrichment.short_title: Knife possession summing-up and good reason defence
key_facts: Police stopped the appellant's car and found scissors on the seat and a kitchen knife under the driver's seat.
The appellant said the knife had been used to start the ignition after keys were lost and he did not know it was in the car when stopped.
He was convicted of possessing a bladed article in a public place without good reason.
The Recorder misdirected the jury on 'knowingly has with him', burden of proof and whether forgetfulness could be a good reason.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction in the Crown Court for an offence under section 139(1) of the 1988 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed and appellant discharged as the summing-up was unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Possession under section 139 requires the defendant knowingly to have the article with him; forgetfulness alone is not a good reason under section 139(4), but the jury should first decide possession and then, on the balance of probabilities, whether the defendant had a good reason in all the circumstances without an unduly restrictive judicial gloss.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'knowingly has with him' for section 139 possession
Whether a mislaid knife remained in the appellant's possession
Burden and standard of proof for the section 139(4) good reason defence
Whether forgetfulness alone or combined with other reasons can amount to good reason

confidence.notes: Comprehensive Court of Appeal review of section 139 law with clear findings on defective directions.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC referral quashes drug and firearms convictions
key_facts: The appellant was convicted in 1996 of possessing a firearm, ammunition and heroin with intent to supply after a police search of his home.
Large quantities of cash, a handgun, ammunition and nearly 5 kg of heroin were found; the appellant claimed he was framed by former business partners.
An earlier appeal was dismissed in 1998, but the CCRC referred the case because of doubts about the 1995 intelligence report.
The Crown conceded convictions were unsafe due to compromised integrity of officers involved in gathering intelligence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal following CCRC reference against 1996 convictions for firearms and drug supply offences.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed with limited public reasons to protect sensitive sources.
enrichment.ratio: Where subsequent investigation casts substantial doubt on the integrity of police intelligence that led to a search and prosecution, and had that information been available the Crown would likely have offered no evidence or full disclosure would have altered the trial, convictions cannot be regarded as safe even if the original trial conduct and PII rulings were unimpeachable on the material then before the court.
legal_issues: Safety of convictions where intelligence-gathering integrity is later undermined
Effect of non-disclosure and public interest immunity on trial fairness
Extent of reasons that may be given when national security limits disclosure

confidence.notes: Judgment deliberately withholds detailed reasoning for public interest reasons; outcome and general basis are clear but underlying evidence is not fully disclosed.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation jurisdiction after defective section 72 notice
key_facts: Simpson pleaded guilty to multiple VAT fraud counts and received a confiscation order of £209,351.34 under section 71 CJA 1988.
He argued the Crown Court lacked jurisdiction because the section 72 notice was defective and because one indicted offence predated the 1995 Act amendments.
A five-judge Court of Appeal held R v Palmer was wrongly decided and followed Sekhon on procedural defects not destroying jurisdiction.
The court also upheld the benefit and realisable assets figures, including £115,000 transferred after the fraud ended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a Crown Court confiscation order, including certified questions on jurisdiction and precedent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; confiscation order upheld and a point of law certified for possible further appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Technical defects in a section 72 confiscation notice do not deprive the Crown Court of jurisdiction where the prosecution clearly initiated confiscation proceedings; section 16(5) of the 1995 Act applies by reference to offences on which confiscation is sought, and a prior court decision may be treated as per incuriam where later authority and fuller argument show the law was misunderstood.
legal_issues: Whether defective section 72 notice removed jurisdiction to make a confiscation order
Whether section 16(5) barred application of 1995 Act amendments where any convicted offence predated commencement
Status of R v Palmer and whether Sekhon could depart from it as per incuriam
Whether £115,000 transferred after the fraud was 'benefit' under section 71(4)

enrichment.short_title: Music compilation licence and copyright estoppel
key_facts: Confetti licensed the track 'Burnin' to Warner for the Heartless Crew compilation album 'Crisp Biscuit' via a signed deal memo headed 'subject to contract'.
Confetti sent a cleared master and a VAT invoice describing the track as already licensed before Warner mixed, manufactured and released the album with a rap overlay.
Confetti later sought to withdraw permission and obtained an interim injunction shortly before release.
Warner mixed 'Burnin' with other tracks and superimposed rap vocals, materially altering the recording.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Copyright infringement and moral rights claim after discharge of an interim injunction restraining release of the compilation.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Warner was licensed by estoppel and/or unilateral contract to use the track on the agreed deal terms.
enrichment.ratio: In the music licensing trade a deal memo marked 'subject to contract' is not itself a binding contract, but sending a cleared track with an invoice stating the track is licensed can amount to an offer accepted by conduct or a representation estopping revocation once the licensee has mixed and manufactured in reliance; 'subject to contract' does not prevent a gratuitous licence or estoppel arising from subsequent conduct.
legal_issues: Whether a signed 'subject to contract' deal memo created a binding licence
Whether sending the track and invoice constituted an offer accepted by Warner's conduct
Whether Confetti were estopped from denying a licence after Warner incurred production costs
Whether overlaying a rap constituted derogatory treatment under section 80

enrichment.short_title: Vexatious litigant order against persistent claimant
key_facts: The Attorney General applied for Mr Ratra to be declared a vexatious litigant under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981.
Mr Ratra had issued numerous claims arising from single incidents, drawing in ever wider circles of defendants including police, solicitors and ombudsmen.
A consultant psychiatrist found paranoid schizophrenia and paranoid personality disorder affecting capacity to manage litigation.
The Official Solicitor acted as litigation friend and conceded the section 42 criteria were met.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for an indefinite civil proceedings order under section 42 after prior interim restrictions.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order made without time limit; future civil proceedings require High Court leave.
enrichment.ratio: Where a person habitually and persistently institutes vexatious civil proceedings without reasonable ground, the court has a discretion to make a section 42 civil proceedings order; that mechanism is preferable to a Part 21 capacity declaration alone because it provides a national filtering process requiring leave before any new claim may be brought.
legal_issues: Whether section 42 criteria were satisfied on the Attorney General's evidence
Whether the court should exercise its discretion to make a civil proceedings order
Whether a Part 21 declaration requiring a litigation friend was an adequate alternative
Effect of the litigant's mental illness on the appropriate protective order

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Shimizu subcontracted cladding works to LBJ under a letter of intent providing for TeCSA adjudication.
An adjudicator awarded LBJ £47,718.39 plus VAT, finding payment was not yet due until a VAT invoice was delivered.
Shimizu served a withholding notice after the decision but before the final date for payment, claiming set-off for defects and delay.
The adjudicator also purported to decide that a DOM/1 contract had been concluded, excluding the LOI price cap.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application for declarations on the meaning and validity of a construction adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted that Shimizu retained the right to serve a withholding notice and that the adjudicator lacked jurisdiction to decide contract formation.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's award of a sum payable only after a VAT invoice does not fetter the payer's statutory and contractual right to serve a valid section 111 withholding notice before the final date for payment; 'without set-off' in the decision addressed only set-offs raised in the adjudication, and where parties agreed their contract was the letter of intent the adjudicator had no jurisdiction to decide otherwise.
legal_issues: Whether 'without set-off' in the adjudicator's decision prevented a later withholding notice
Whether a dispute over future withholding rights was referred to adjudication
Whether the adjudicator had jurisdiction to decide the contractual basis of the parties' relationship
Whether TeCSA rules 28 and 33 barred the court from construing the decision
